trial.ground_truth: Four concurrent long queries occupy all four inventory pool slots
trial.predicted_root_cause: inventory-service issues `SELECT pg_sleep(2)` queries that block for 2 seconds per call. With a pool of only 4 connections (pool_max=4), four concurrent sleeps occupy every slot (pool_available=0), so ordinary /products queries must wait for a free connection. They exceed the 0.80s pool acquisition timeout and fail with `PoolTimeout: couldn't get a connection after 0.80 sec`, returning HTTP 500 from inventory-service, which the gateway surfaces as HTTP 502 to the client (49.18% error rate at both gateway and inventory-service). pg_stat_statements shows two pg_sleep statements executed 164 and 745 times with mean exec times ~2.0s and ~1.2s, and live pg_stat_activity shows four active inventory-service backends in PgSleep/Timeout state. Latency (~800ms p95) matches the pool-timeout plus queueing behavior, not raw query cost. The shared postgres instance is not globally degraded: order-service, payment-service, user-service and gateway all keep pool_available>=1-3 with zero or negligible errors.

regression_risks: Increasing pool_max without bounding query/statement timeouts could exhaust postgres max_connections and shift the failure to the DB.
Removing a pg_sleep call that is injected debug/simulation code may silently change app semantics if it also enforced ordering or throttling.
Relying on restart alone leaves no guard (timeout budget/circuit breaker), so recurrence remains possible on next slow dependency.
critic_result.test_sufficiency: Insufficient to fully confirm the fix: no code diff or call-site grep evidence is supplied, no test artifact reproduces PoolTimeout under pg_sleep, and the after-window is a single operator-observed 20s sample showing error_pct=0%. A controlled test confirming PoolTimeout before and its absence after removing/gating pg_sleep (or a bounded-timeout assertion) would be required to prove the causal patch.
critic_result.verification_summary: Diagnosis mechanism is well-supported for the observed outage window. Before: pg_stat_activity (E-4c16d16fe3d14bcf, before snapshot) shows 4 active inventory-service backends running SELECT pg_sleep(2), wait_event PgSleep/Timeout — exactly saturating a pool_max=4. Service logs (E-1220607725464ec8) show inventory-service /products returning 500 PoolTimeout after 0.80s on the same trace_ids the gateway reports as 502, and metrics (E-1b93cd05964f45c1, E-f3d72880c4bc4fbe) show 49-50% errors co-located at inventory-service and gateway only, with order/payment/user near-zero. This refutes a global postgres bottleneck and cache-miss origin, and supports connection-pool starvation caused by long-running sleeps. However two caveats prevent full VERIFIED. (1) The after window (E-f678cdf8a1264987, E-3ee7d842694a4a87, E-8577bca8353445fe) shows inventory-service pool_available=4, errors 0%, and NO pg_sleep in activity — i.e., regression was observed only after the pg_sleep calls stopped; the supplied evidence never shows the pg_sleep call site in code, so removing/gating that call remains inferred, not directly read. (2) Cumulative pg_stat_statements counters and after-window deltas do not by themselves prove current sleep activity; the live active PgSleep sessions plus concurrent 500s in the before window are the actual causal link, and that link is observational. Also note inventory-service health was "unavailable" in the before snapshot (no pool stats), so its exhaustion state is inferred from triage S3 (pool_available=0) rather than direct measured before health. Patch decision is NO_CODE_PATCH, so diagnosis verification does not assert any recovery action was performed; the after-window return to health was operator-observed, not an AI patch.

diagnosis.root_cause: inventory-service issues `SELECT pg_sleep(2)` queries that block for 2 seconds per call. With a pool of only 4 connections (pool_max=4), four concurrent sleeps occupy every slot (pool_available=0), so ordinary /products queries must wait for a free connection. They exceed the 0.80s pool acquisition timeout and fail with `PoolTimeout: couldn't get a connection after 0.80 sec`, returning HTTP 500 from inventory-service, which the gateway surfaces as HTTP 502 to the client (49.18% error rate at both gateway and inventory-service). pg_stat_statements shows two pg_sleep statements executed 164 and 745 times with mean exec times ~2.0s and ~1.2s, and live pg_stat_activity shows four active inventory-service backends in PgSleep/Timeout state. Latency (~800ms p95) matches the pool-timeout plus queueing behavior, not raw query cost. The shared postgres instance is not globally degraded: order-service, payment-service, user-service and gateway all keep pool_available>=1-3 with zero or negligible errors.

regression_risks: Increasing pool_max without bounding query/statement timeouts could exhaust postgres max_connections and shift the failure to the DB.
Removing a pg_sleep call that is injected debug/simulation code may silently change app semantics if it also enforced ordering or throttling.
Relying on restart alone leaves no guard (timeout budget/circuit breaker), so recurrence remains possible on next slow dependency.
critic.test_sufficiency: Insufficient to fully confirm the fix: no code diff or call-site grep evidence is supplied, no test artifact reproduces PoolTimeout under pg_sleep, and the after-window is a single operator-observed 20s sample showing error_pct=0%. A controlled test confirming PoolTimeout before and its absence after removing/gating pg_sleep (or a bounded-timeout assertion) would be required to prove the causal patch.
critic.verification_summary: Diagnosis mechanism is well-supported for the observed outage window. Before: pg_stat_activity (E-4c16d16fe3d14bcf, before snapshot) shows 4 active inventory-service backends running SELECT pg_sleep(2), wait_event PgSleep/Timeout — exactly saturating a pool_max=4. Service logs (E-1220607725464ec8) show inventory-service /products returning 500 PoolTimeout after 0.80s on the same trace_ids the gateway reports as 502, and metrics (E-1b93cd05964f45c1, E-f3d72880c4bc4fbe) show 49-50% errors co-located at inventory-service and gateway only, with order/payment/user near-zero. This refutes a global postgres bottleneck and cache-miss origin, and supports connection-pool starvation caused by long-running sleeps. However two caveats prevent full VERIFIED. (1) The after window (E-f678cdf8a1264987, E-3ee7d842694a4a87, E-8577bca8353445fe) shows inventory-service pool_available=4, errors 0%, and NO pg_sleep in activity — i.e., regression was observed only after the pg_sleep calls stopped; the supplied evidence never shows the pg_sleep call site in code, so removing/gating that call remains inferred, not directly read. (2) Cumulative pg_stat_statements counters and after-window deltas do not by themselves prove current sleep activity; the live active PgSleep sessions plus concurrent 500s in the before window are the actual causal link, and that link is observational. Also note inventory-service health was "unavailable" in the before snapshot (no pool stats), so its exhaustion state is inferred from triage S3 (pool_available=0) rather than direct measured before health. Patch decision is NO_CODE_PATCH, so diagnosis verification does not assert any recovery action was performed; the after-window return to health was operator-observed, not an AI patch.

alternative_explanations: pg_sleep is a synthetic load generator rather than the real defect; pool_max=4 with a 0.80s acquisition timeout may be genuinely undersized for steady /products traffic, so removing pg_sleep could mask but not fix capacity issues.
A slow/blocking /products query or lock contention (not pg_sleep) could have held connections; the observed PgSleep could be coincidental background traffic.
Gateway 502s might originate from an independent gateway timeout/circuit behavior layered on top of inventory-service 500s, rather than purely propagating upstream errors.
